title: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban
description: A judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building
body: A judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building last week by the president.A District of Columbia court issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, meaning CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days, after ruling the move "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".The three outlets launched a legal challenge after their reporters had their passes for the White House confiscated and were denied access.The Trump administration defended the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security - an argument the court rejected.The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.Judge Timothy Kelly ruled, external CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban.He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement.The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds."In its defence of the ban, the Trump administration cited a number of articles published by the outlets, including some about construction at the White House, including work on a new ballroom.The judge said that "in most cases" the stories the White House took issue with were written by journalists who "did not even hold card passes" - and in the remaining cases, the Trump administration did not demonstrate "reason to believe that the reporter's possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified".In its original filing, the Trump administration cited declarations from defence department officials supporting the ban - but the judge said they had "no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here".Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, told CNN, external: "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law."On Monday, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties in protest at the ban. The arrangement sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - also filed a legal brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's lawsuit.Trump frequently criticises news organisations, and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

schema.headline: Judge temporarily overturns Trump's White House media ban

title: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
description: The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it
body: The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination.Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face.Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity. However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation.Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures"."International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added.Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks.Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector."We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month.Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday. "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman.He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology".He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes"."We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added.Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches.  Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole".He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety".    "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added. "But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale."Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure."All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology.Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI. Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia. The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

schema.headline: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards

title: Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
description: Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled.The discount supermarket chain fac
body: Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled.The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling. Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions.Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has contacted Lidl for comment. The ruling, which can still be appealed against, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design".It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs. In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed against.And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals.However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025.The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they were practical products rather than works of art – an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time.  Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products"."To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added.Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry.Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats.

schema.headline: Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules

title: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
description: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide du
body: Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran. The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew". He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time". Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions,  calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable". "What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday."Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US. US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageUS sailors arrive in Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at seaSuicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.A study, external of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

schema.headline: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says

title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
description: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gamblin
body: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work.This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items.The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable".A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms."Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year.Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair"."The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said."Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided"."Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said."We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

schema.headline: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes

title: Laver Cup 2026: Carlos Alcaraz on US Open run, injury and Jannik Sinner rivalry
description: Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3.34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling.Carlos Alcaraz is not most p
body: Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3.34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling.Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.After his loss to Ben Shelton - a match that played out over a gruelling four hours and 28 minutes - the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin on his face.Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament for over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day.He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before."The quarter-final was great - it was a gift for me," Alcaraz told BBC Sport before this week's Laver Cup in London."I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling."The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history, and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours.Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am."I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late."The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed."I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm or whatever would be better."Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury.Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury.The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy".He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September.The team tournament pits Europe - captained by Yannick Noah - against a United States team overseen by Andre Agassi."When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said."We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well."Alcaraz and Italy's Sinner split eight Grand Slam titles between them from 2024 and 2025, establishing a generational rivalry in the process.They have only met once this year because of injuries, with Sinner winning their sole meeting in the Monte Carlo Masters final to become world number one."I have text him not too much, but a few times when he has been winning everything, mostly at the beginning of the year," Alcaraz added."I miss him, I miss seeing him around, playing against him. He pushes me to be a better player."People will be waiting for those matches, so I think it's going to be better."

schema.headline: Laver Cup 2026: Carlos Alcaraz on US Open run, injury and Jannik Sinner rivalry

title: Football news: Anthony Gordon urges England to stop trying to replicate Spain
description: Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the English "DNA" but the Three Lions could win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replica
body: Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the English "DNA" but the Three Lions could win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replicate Spain".The Barcelona winger was speaking at St George's Park as the England squad prepare to take on world champions Spain on Saturday - their first match together since the World Cup.England lost their semi-final 2-1 to Argentina, before beating France 6-4 in the bronze medal match.Ending on a high meant England achieved their best finish in a World Cup since 1966.But many have criticised the manner in which England were beaten by Argentina, after head coach Thomas Tuchel substituted goalscorer Gordon and went to a back five.The tactical tweak invited pressure, with Enzo Fernandez equalising before Lautaro Martinez scored a stoppage-time winner.Gordon said that he had "never felt worse", after the game and believes that the "scar" left by defeat may mean the England squad take a different approach in the next tournament."[The] scar doesn't have to be a negative one because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments," Gordon said."We can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them - we're English and we have our own strengths which they don't have, so maybe we start playing the way we're good at."Gordon moved to Barcelona from Newcastle for £69.3m in the summer.He says that the experience of playing in La Liga - with and against some of Spain's top stars - has made him realise just how different the nation's approach is to football.He is not convinced English players can be taught to play more like the Spanish, with their intricate possession-based game."I'm speaking from a point of view where I feel like we are trying to replicate Spain," Gordon said."Because I'm in Spain, I know we have just as good players, but they have different qualities, so why are you trying to make those players the same as the Spanish players? Because the Spanish players lack the things that we have and vice versa."England have lost two consecutive European Championship finals, and been beaten by France and Argentina in the past two World Cups.Those outcomes have led to repeated questions about whether the team are good enough at controlling possession against elite nations.Spain won the World Cup by beating Argentina and dominated with 65% of the ball in the final, restricting opponents led by Lionel Messi to just two shots in 120 minutes of play, neither of which hit the target.Spain's particular style will test England again this weekend, and the Wembley hosts will look to find a response - but perhaps not by copying their opponents."It's not in the English DNA," Gordon said."I'm not sure it's something that can be taught because now I think, playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different."I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think I'm not sure how you've seen that."It's the way they're built. I don't know whether it is something that maybe we can't ever put a name to, but they're definitely built different."Gordon's goal in the semi-final capped what was an impressive tournament for the 25-year-old and briefly had England supporters dreaming of World Cup glory.The winger started five of England's games and also provided four assists.He was taken off 17 minutes after putting the Three Lions ahead against Argentina and says that he was surprised to be substituted.He says that after scoring he plays "off adrenaline" and "goes into an untouchable mode of confidence"."It makes me feel on top of the world, especially in that moment on that stage. I felt really good," he said."But as a winger, to be honest, I come off most games. It's normal [for wingers]."Obviously that substitution was different but in that moment probably yeah, but in general as a winger I expect it a lot of the time."England had battled to a 3-2 win over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium, where they played with 10 men for over 35 minutes after Jarell Quansah's red card.According to Gordon, the manner of that last-16 victory was a factor in the players' thinking when trying to get over the line against Argentina.The winger also suggested that the team did not match the performances that they were creating in training.If they had, Gordon says, they "would have dominated everyone".He defended Tuchel's "more safe and more defensive" tactics, which sparked external criticism and in-camp disappointment."We shouldn't try and blame one man who's obviously trying his best and trying to win the cup for us all," Gordon said."As players, we could have done more to take the initiative to control the [Argentina] game. I think if we do that the manager doesn't make the decision [to use a back five]."For me, we had the best team, we had the best players on the pitch in that semi-final, and in the last 20 minutes we didn't play the best football."That's something the manager can't really affect from the sideline, so I think as a group everyone together should take responsibility."

schema.headline: Football news: Anthony Gordon urges England to stop trying to replicate Spain

title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
description: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN Gene
body: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason"."The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year."All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that". Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be."Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well."Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said.In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of Hamas.In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year. Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza. But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

schema.headline: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction

title: New vocational GCSE subjects to be introduced in schools
description: New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.The new subjects could include
body: New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.  Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels, which colleges are teaching from autumn 2027, and T-levels.The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications. Education Secretary Lucy Powell argued the new vocational GCSEs would give young people a "stronger connection" to careers, while the prime minister said it was a change from a "one size fits all" education system. Powell told BBC Breakfast schools would be able to specialise in subjects relevant to the jobs available in their local areas, adding that she wanted to improve the "esteem, respect and recognition" of the current qualifications.Asked whether there would be dedicated funding to help schools cover the cost of the new qualifications, she said the government would "work with the sector to make sure this is absolutely deliverable", and that ministers would "make sure any funding needed is made available".VCSEs, external, a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027.Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​.Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer.Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10.Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject. This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs. Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator.  The standards for the new vocational GCSEs will be national.Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs. She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects.   Martin Haworth, executive headteacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility. He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning.New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29. This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas. Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities. He said there was a  "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit. The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff. David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused".Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications.While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well intentioned" but without making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people. He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure more support was needed from employers. The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds. Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements. Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow education secretary said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures"."Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most," she said.The Liberal Democrats also warned the new vocational GCSEs should not become a "pipeline" directing disadvantaged pupils away from more academic subjects.

schema.headline: New vocational GCSE subjects to be introduced in schools

title: NHS staff investigated over access to dead teenager's medical records
description: The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed
body: The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed inappropriately for years after his death.Paula McGowan, whose 18-year-old autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Bristol Foundation NHS Trust may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year.Three nursing staff are under formal investigation, while a doctor who no longer works for the trust has self-referred to the General Medical Council. Another member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.The trust said it was "deeply sorry" for any stress and anxiety caused.It said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.It is the latest case involving concerns that NHS staff may have accessed patient records without a legitimate professional reason. In July the head of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, issued a "stark warning" that staff could face the sack or even prison for doing so.Recent high-profile examples include the victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.This month an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years.Oliver, who had a mild learning disability and epilepsy, died in 2016 at Southmead Hospital in Bristol after being given anti-psychotic medication that his family had repeatedly warned he should not receive.After requesting information about his medical records, his mother was told that 38 people had accessed the data since his death, with 637 items viewed and 67 printed off.Most access was appropriate and linked to complaints, legal proceedings, and the coroner's inquest into his death.But three nursing staff not involved in his care are currently under formal investigation after initial inquiries could find no evidence they had a legitimate reason to view her son's records.A fourth member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.McGowan said she was told that one nurse wanted to view the files as they had a general interest in anti-psychotic drugs and the care of patients with a learning disability.The trust is also looking into 13 other cases involving former staff, including doctors, nurses and clerical workers, to establish if that access was appropriate or not.One doctor, who no longer works at the trust, has already referred themselves to the medical regulator, the GMC, after being approached by the hospital.Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete". "Every patient and family has the right to expect that their personal information will be treated with care, respect and confidentiality," said Prof Steve Hams, the trust's chief nursing and improvement officer."Any concern that records may have been accessed without a legitimate reason is something we take extremely seriously."The trust said that, should any staff misconduct be identified, "appropriate action will be taken through the relevant processes". NHS medical records can contain highly sensitive personal information, ranging from test results and hospital discharge summaries to details of prescriptions and medications.That extends well beyond the information available to patients through the NHS app and may include safeguarding concerns, risk assessments, correspondence between healthcare professionals and detailed consultation notes.There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access. Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information.Doctors, nurses and other healthcare staff often need fast access, particularly in emergencies. However, they should only view confidential information when they have a legitimate work-related reason and the right authorisation.IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when.NHS England said any instance of staff looking at records without a valid reason would be "wholly unacceptable, a disgraceful breach of patients' trust and against the law"."We have been crystal clear that staff could face disciplinary action for any breaches, including the loss of their job and potential criminal prosecution," added a spokesman.

schema.headline: NHS staff investigated over access to dead teenager's medical records

title: Heat risk in sport: Are chances of death and serious illness growing with extreme temperatures?
description: 'Tragic but avoidable' - how serious is heat-death risk in sport?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Met Office has confirmed that 2026 was t
body: 'Tragic but avoidable' - how serious is heat-death risk in sport?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Met Office has confirmed that 2026 was the UK's hottest summer, and many other countries around the world have also dealt with extreme heatByDaniel AustinBBC Sport senior journalistOn Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates.After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead.In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away".Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer.By noon on the day Vunilagi became ill, the temperature in Fukuoka - where Kyuden Voltex are based - had risen to 35C. The humidity was more than 75%.In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C.No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days.So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change?'Extreme heat should be treated like lightning'There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026.Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C.Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages.This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare.Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation.But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase."We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto."People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'."That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jakub Mensik was helped by rival Mariano Navone after collapsing at the end of a five-set match which lasted four hours and 41 minutes, and was played in more than 32C heatThough the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme."Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr."It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away."We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens."'Players need protecting from themselves'One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health."I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association."And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes."It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing."It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training."World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale.But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches."If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day."Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors."It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, By early August, the Japan Meteorological Agency had recorded 4,727 instances of 'extremely hot' temperatures across the country since the start of 2026Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports.On 5 June 2026, the Japan Rugby Football Union (JRFU) warned clubs heatstroke was an increasing concern during the summer, and told teams safety should be the overriding priority when planning summer training camps.'Every single death is one too many'Heatstroke is a sudden, dangerous health condition which occurs when the body overheats and can no longer cool itself.This can damage the organs, cause the intestines to release toxins and potentially be fatal within little more than an hour.Symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion and slurring."Heatstroke is 100% preventable, so every single death is one too many," says Orr."It's not the case that athletes can handle heat better because of their fitness."And the bigger the body the faster it heats up, so bigger bodies are more vulnerable as well. Moving that mass around takes a lot of energy. "So while yes, professional athletes are extraordinarily fit, that doesn't save them when the issue of concern is cooling off the body."Amateur athletes playing for the love of the game can be at risk too."Whatever the elite level does, we'll see it trickle down into grassroots," says Day. "And that's why it's crucial that the elite level of every sport sets the right example because the kids, the players of tomorrow, will absolutely copy whatever they see their heroes doing."

schema.headline: Heat risk in sport: Are chances of death and serious illness growing with extreme temperatures?

title: Newspaper headlines: 'RAF jet crash escape' and 'Tories to cut benefits'
description: Many of the front pages focus on the Conservative party's promise to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments
body: Many of the front pages focus on the Conservative party's promise to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and betting. The Daily Mail's headline is "Kemi's ruthless crackdown on benefits street", external. The Daily Telegraph says the Tories want to stop joblessness being what is referred to as a "lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered", external.The front page of the Daily Mirror carries a photograph of the moment two RAF pilots ejected from a jet before it crashed on Anglesey in North Wales, external. They were taking part in a training exercise when they were forced to parachute from the plane - which, the paper reports, then "plummeted nose-first into a field" and caused a "huge fireball". The paper's headline is "Miracle no one was killed".According to the Daily Telegraph, talks about the future of the Elgin marbles have collapsed, external. Greece reopened negotiations with the British Museum in 2021 as part of efforts to repatriate the ancient sculptures. But the paper says "it is understood negotiations are effectively over" as Greek representatives are frustrated by a lack of progress.The Times says mounted cavalry might have an advantage in modern warfare, external, a century on after tanks replaced horses on the battlefield. Last year, a Ukrainian infantry company in Donetsk reported that Russian forces had started to use horses and donkeys to carry soldiers and supplies to avoid detection by drones. And the paper says the UK's Household Mounted Cavalry regiment conducted trials over the summer, with officials saying in some situations, such as woodland, there's a better chance of getting from A to B with a horse, than with a Challenger 2 tank.And the boss of Timpsons says his company has seen a 680% increase in people asking for extra holes in their belts this year,, external reports the Daily Mail. He believes the demand is down to the popularity of weight loss jabs.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'RAF jet crash escape' and 'Tories to cut benefits'

title: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'
description: A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in
body: A Harry Potter And The Cursed Child producer has said the rising cost of living made it "literally impossible" to retain the play's original format in two parts.The production has been cut down to a single three-hour show and is set to re-open in the West End next month."The cost of living has gone up 30-40% since the pandemic, including running shows," producer Sonia Friedman said in comments reported by media at a launch event. "The only way we could continue to run it as a two-parter would be by charging an amount for the tickets that would be unaffordable and inaccessible." The two-part play, a sequel to JK Rowling's books, premiered in the West End in 2016 and closed on 20 September.The changes to the West End production follow the 2021 relaunch of the play as a single show on Broadway in New York City. "The pandemic, the cost of living and the wars going on around the world accelerated that decision in New York, and that's where we are now with London," Friedman said."Of course we'll miss it but it was absolutely the right call and we've got a beautiful alternate version that we're very proud of."Director John Tiffany said at the launch event that he and writer Jack Thorne - who also wrote acclaimed Netflix series Adolescence - had to be "dragged, kicking and screaming to make the one-parter" due to the success of their original script, the Times reported.However, Tiffany said the new version meant "more people are going to get to see this show and not have to pay a fortune for it", according to The Stage.The play takes place 19 years after the final book and follows Harry's son Albus Severus as he arrives at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.The production has been seen by more than 14 million people around the world, including over 2.5 million in London.The reimagined one-part production will retain some of its original cast, including David Ricardo-Pearce as Harry Potter, Thomas Aldridge as Ron Weasley and Naana Agyei Ampadu as Hermione Granger. New actors have been cast in the roles of Albus Potter, Ginny Potter, Rose Granger-Weasley, Draco Malfoy and Scorpius Malfoy.

schema.headline: Harry Potter play producer says cost of living made two-part show 'impossible'

title: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs across Scotland
description: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human traffickingImage caption, One of the targeted sites was a nail salon in GlasgowByS
body: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human traffickingImage caption, One of the targeted sites was a nail salon in GlasgowByScotland home affairs correspondentOne of Scotland's biggest police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms.About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations.In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders.Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime.The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year.Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth £26m were seized.Subsequent inquiries linked a single Vietnamese crime group to about a third of the farms, with months of planning leading up to Wednesday's raids.Det Supt Stevie Bertram said: "This was by far the biggest human trafficking investigation that Police Scotland has ever run."We wanted to disrupt and absolutely cripple that organisation."We wanted to do it all in one day and I think it's been a huge success. Essentially, they won't be able to function."All of the targets of this operation have been arrested and they are the ones we believe are running that operation."Figure caption, Cannabis plants were found at several locations across ScotlandPolice Scotland officers arrested individuals in Birmingham as part of Wednesday's enforcement action, which was carried out with support from Home Office Immigration Enforcement and His Majesty's Revenue and Customs."We think the group runs across the UK and internationally," said Bertram."We've met with regional crime teams from up and down England and Wales and Ireland, to look at what's happening across the country."Officers from the National Crime Agency based in Hanoi have been liaising with the authorities in Vietnam.Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, A large number of plants were found in a raid in DundeeThe addresses raided by the police included a tenement flat in Edinburgh's South Clerk Street, a five-minute walk from one of the capital's busiest police stations.Three rooms were crammed with plants growing behind tarpaulin screens under bright lights.A box of seedlings was discovered in the kitchen. There were signs of occupation, though no-one was in the flat when the police forced entry.In Dundee, a cannabis operation discovered in two neighbouring flats had been extended into a shared loft.The police will now try to establish whether the people arrested include victims of human trafficking."Vietnamese nationals are still the highest nationality that we see being exploited in Scotland" said Bertram."A lot of hard work and investigation will go on from today."We'll examine mobiles, data, paperwork to make sure that if there is a victim of human trafficking, they're quickly identified as a victim."

schema.headline: Police arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs across Scotland
